situation.s13_after_antietam.text: Lincoln challenges McClellan's assessment of relative risk and urges movement against the enemy. He distinguishes between a suggestion and an order. The letter records presidential pressure; it does not make the commander's army march or prove that its supply objections are false.
situation.s13_after_antietam.title: Lincoln asks the army to move
situation.s13_altoona_governors.text: The governors' address supports the preliminary proclamation and the government's prosecution of the war. It is the signatories' statement. It neither changes state quotas by itself nor proves that every governor agrees with it.
situation.s13_altoona_governors.title: The governors address the President
situation.s13_arms_and_contracts.text: Ripley reports that the Henry and Spencer arms require special ammunition and that the field trials remain limited. He objects to added weight, ammunition variety and price, and advises against the proposed purchases. His assessment is an ordnance recommendation, not proof that the weapons cannot work.
situation.s13_arms_and_contracts.title: Magazine arms and contracts
situation.s13_army_of_virginia.text: Lincoln’s order consolidates the forces of Frémont, Banks and McDowell, including Sturgis’s Washington troops, into an Army of Virginia under Pope. It specifies three corps, their commanders and the army’s purposes. The order does not establish that every commander accepts the arrangement.
situation.s13_army_of_virginia.title: Three commands in one army
situation.s13_army_will_not_move.text: Lincoln's General War Order No. 1 sets 22 February for a general movement of the land and naval forces. It names the main commands expected to be ready and holds department heads and commanders responsible. Issuing the order is distinct from any army actually moving.
situation.s13_army_will_not_move.title: A date for a general movement
situation.s13_bond_agent.text: A dated notice from Jay Cooke's office says that the Secretary of the Treasury has appointed him subscription agent for five-twenty bonds and that he is prepared to furnish them. This is the agent's announcement; it does not establish total sales or the commission paid.
situation.s13_bond_agent.title: The subscription agent for bonds
situation.s13_buell_east_tennessee.text: Buell urges a movement first toward Nashville and describes supply and route constraints. Halleck says the government wants East Tennessee occupied promptly while Nashville is covered and a return into Kentucky prevented. These are competing operational judgments. The edition prints Halleck’s reply on 23 October but notes that its true date appears to be 22 October.
situation.s13_buell_east_tennessee.title: The objective in East Tennessee
situation.s13_cabinet_remonstrance.text: In his entry of 31 August, Welles describes Chase asking him to sign a paper against McClellan which Stanton had drawn. Welles opposes McClellan’s command but declines to sign and proposes full cabinet consultation. This is one participant’s record, not evidence of a unanimous recommendation.
situation.s13_cabinet_remonstrance.title: The paper against McClellan
situation.s13_committee_and_stone.text: Lincoln tells the Senate that Stone was imprisoned under his general authority. He declines to disclose the evidence, promises charges and a trial, and attributes the delay to the difficulty of withdrawing officers and witnesses from active service. This is the President's explanation, not a finding of guilt.
situation.s13_committee_and_stone.title: The Senate asks about Stone
situation.s13_compensated_emancipation.t: Lincoln asks Congress to support federal aid to a state that adopts gradual abolition of slavery. His message leaves acceptance to the state. It proposes an offer; it does not enact state abolition or show that any state has accepted.
situation.s13_confiscation_and_militia_a: The confiscation legislation declares freedom in specified circumstances and forbids military or naval personnel from deciding claims to fugitives or surrendering them to claimants. The separate Militia Act authorizes Black service and specifies its terms. These laws do not prove that a particular person has enlisted or been paid.
situation.s13_dakota_war.text: Lincoln asks Pope to forward the complete records of the convictions and further particulars if the records are insufficient. Requesting the records is a review step; it is not an execution order or a finding that every conviction is sound.
situation.s13_dakota_war.title: The Dakota trial records
situation.s13_emancipation_cabinet_draft: Carpenter records Lincoln's later account that Seward advised postponing publication of the emancipation draft until military success could support it. Lincoln did not remember the exact date in that conversation. This report of a recollection is not a verbatim July cabinet minute.
situation.s13_emancipation_preliminary.t: The proclamation announces freedom on 1 January for people enslaved in states or designated parts then in rebellion. It also directs immediate enforcement of the March military return prohibition and July confiscation clauses. The announced future act and the immediate instructions are different provisions.
situation.s13_fredericksburg_bridges.tex: Woodbury reports that missing harness, teamsters and horses have delayed the pontoon train. His earlier readiness forecast and the army's arrival at Falmouth are different events. The correspondence does not settle every later claim about responsibility for the delay.
situation.s13_fremont_department.text: The enclosed relief order is to reach Frémont through Curtis. Lincoln directs that it be held if Frémont has just fought and won a battle, is fighting, or stands immediately before an expected battle. Hunter is to receive his enclosure only after Frémont receives his.
situation.s13_fremont_department.title: The Western Department's command
situation.s13_fremont_proclamation.text: The Western Department has declared martial law throughout Missouri. Its proclamation declares freedom for people enslaved by the opponents it describes and threatens shooting after court-martial. These are separate clauses of the proclamation.
situation.s13_fremont_proclamation.title: Frémont's proclamation
situation.s13_general_in_chief_1861.text: The War Department's order places Scott on the retired list on his application and directs McClellan to assume command of the United States Army. The headquarters remains in Washington. The order does not settle the private dispute over how voluntary the retirement was.
situation.s13_general_in_chief_1862.text: Lincoln's order assigns Halleck command of the whole land forces as general-in-chief and directs him to come to Washington when he can safely leave his department. Assignment is distinct from arrival and assumption of command.
situation.s13_grant_rumour.text: By direction of the President, the Adjutant-General asks Halleck to ascertain and report whether Grant left his command without proper authority, for how long, whether he supplied proper returns, and what unauthorized acts he committed, if any. The inquiry requests evidence; it does not enter the allegation as a personal trait.
situation.s13_grant_rumour.title: Particulars about Grant
situation.s13_greeley_reply.text: Lincoln replies to Greeley that his paramount object in the struggle is saving the Union. He distinguishes his official duty from his personal wish that all people could be free. The letter is a public answer, not publication of the private policy draft.
situation.s13_greeley_reply.title: A reply to Greeley
situation.s13_hampton_roads_scare.text: Welles retrospectively describes Stanton arguing that McClellan’s Peninsula movement must be abandoned and fearing that Burnside would be captured. Welles says Burnside was beyond the ironclad’s draft and expresses confidence in the Monitor. These are competing judgments reported by Welles, not a guarantee about future naval movement.
situation.s13_hampton_roads_scare.title: The ironclad alarm
situation.s13_harrisons_landing_letter.t: McClellan's letter from Harrison's Landing argues against confiscation and forcible abolition and asks for a general-in-chief. Its political recommendations are his, rather than the government's policy or the reading public's judgment.
situation.s13_hunter_order.text: Lincoln reproduces Hunter’s order declaring enslaved people free in Georgia, Florida and South Carolina, and declares the emancipation provision void. He reserves the commander-in-chief question to himself and renews his appeal for compensated abolition. His proclamation does not revoke every camp regulation.
situation.s13_hunter_order.title: Hunter's declaration of freedom
situation.s13_maryland_legislature_autum: Cameron directs Banks to prevent a secession act by the Maryland legislature, using arrests if necessary and leaving the time and manner to Banks. The instruction records the government's intention; it does not establish that legislators had agreed to secede.
situation.s13_mcclellan_relief.text: The President directs McClellan’s relief and names Burnside to succeed him. He also directs related command changes and gives the general-in-chief discretion about when to issue the order. Its drafting, issue, delivery and the field change of command are distinct.
situation.s13_mcclellan_relief.title: The order changing army command
situation.s13_military_arrests.text: The presidential proclamation subjects specified rebels and those discouraging enlistment, resisting militia drafts or giving aid and comfort to the enemy to military proceedings. It suspends the writ for persons it describes in military custody. It does not establish the guilt of every person arrested.
situation.s13_military_arrests.title: Military arrests and the writ
situation.s13_new_orleans_command.text: Butler's General Orders No. 28 threatens women who insult United States officers or soldiers with treatment as prostitutes soliciting. The order states the commander's policy. It does not establish any particular assault or the extent of enforcement.
situation.s13_new_orleans_command.title: The occupation order at New Orleans
situation.s13_norfolk.text: Stanton reports that a tug surrendered from Norfolk and that its people describe evacuation and dismantling of the navy yard. He says an attack on Sewell’s Point is planned by the naval and army commanders. The deserters’ account is intelligence; the planned attack is not a report that Norfolk has fallen.
situation.s13_norfolk.title: The operation at Norfolk
situation.s13_peninsula_withdrawal.text: Halleck orders the Army of the Potomac withdrawn to Aquia Creek and directs that the sick leave first. McClellan protests the withdrawal. Their disagreement is about the army's destination and cooperation with the forces near Washington; it is not a direct move available to the President.
situation.s13_peninsula_withdrawal.title: The order to leave the Peninsula
situation.s13_railroad_dispute.text: Haupt recalls that Sturgis stopped four trains and threatened him with arrest. He reproduces Halleck's instruction that military officers must not interfere with railroad operations. Haupt's account explains his own actions; its claim about troops delayed is not an independently measured battle outcome.
situation.s13_railroad_dispute.title: The stopped railroad trains
situation.s13_recruiting_call.text: Lincoln tells Stanton not to issue what could be read as an additional troop demand beyond the recent call. He stresses filling old regiments and permits enrollment and drafts if Stanton thinks that will help, with practicable credit against a state's volunteer quota.
situation.s13_recruiting_call.title: Recruits for the old regiments
situation.s13_recruiting_closed.text: The War Department discontinues the volunteer recruiting service, orders detached recruiters back to their regiments and directs that the offices close and their public property be sold. This is an instruction to the establishment, not proof that every office has complied.
situation.s13_recruiting_closed.title: Recruiting offices closed
situation.s13_river_squadron.text: Mahan's detailed account places the flotilla's transfer to the Navy on 1 October and its designation as the Mississippi Squadron. An earlier passage in the same book places the transfer in July. The legal effective date must be checked against the transfer instrument before this account supplies a command change.
situation.s13_river_squadron.title: The river flotilla and the Navy
situation.s13_treasury_notes.text: Chase's account of the financial emergency says the New York banks suspended specie payments on 30 December, followed by most banks and the government for its circulating notes. He describes the alternatives to a national currency as borrowing on increasingly unfavorable terms or relying on bank credit. His report is a later explanation of the crisis.
situation.s13_treasury_notes.title: The Treasury and specie payments
situation.s13_trent_affair.text: Seward's reply offers to release Mason, Slidell and their secretaries. He distinguishes Wilkes's action from an instruction by the government and bases release on the failure to bring the seized persons before a prize court.
situation.s13_trent_affair.title: The Trent correspondence
situation.s13_vicksburg_river_1862.text: Mahan describes the Gulf fleet and accompanying troops going downriver because the river was falling and sickness was increasing. He distinguishes the Gulf fleet’s withdrawal from Davis’s later movement toward Helena. This retrospective history does not itself supply the Navy Department’s instruction.
situation.s13_vicksburg_river_1862.title: The fleets at Vicksburg
situation.s13_war_department_report.text: The Richmond Daily Dispatch reproduces a New York Tribune account that Lincoln recalled copies of the War Department report and intended to remove its passage on emancipation and arming enslaved people. This is an attributed newspaper report; it is not a cabinet transcript.
situation.s13_war_department_secretary.t: Lincoln offers Cameron the mission to Russia. Cameron's reply accepts the new position. The correspondence presents the change as a resignation and diplomatic appointment; it does not itself prove every allegation about War Department contracts.
situation.s13_war_orders_march_1862.text: The March orders organize the Army of the Potomac into corps. The special order of 11 March leaves McClellan his own department, puts the consolidated Department of the Mississippi under Halleck and creates the Mountain Department under Frémont. These are separate organizational acts.
situation.s13_washington_cover.text: Lincoln explains that he detained McDowell because the arrangement for covering Washington had changed. He asks McClellan to account for a discrepancy between the strength figures supplied to him. The letter states Lincoln's case; neither figure is silently adopted as the army's true strength.
situation.s13_washington_cover.title: The force left for Washington
situation.s13_kentucky_camp_protest.titl: Kentucky asks that the camp leave
situation.s13_kentucky_camp_protest.text: Lincoln’s reply quotes Magoffin’s request of 19 August that the federal military force leave Kentucky. Lincoln declines, describing his own understanding of its composition and the wishes of Unionists. These are the two men’s positions, not a measured poll or a certified strength return.
situation.s13_atlantic_squadron_division: The Atlantic squadron is to divide

Welles appoints Goldsborough and describes an intended division of the Atlantic squadron. Goldsborough is to command the whole until Du Pont arrives, then the waters of Virginia and North Carolina, excluding the Potomac. The September instruction and the eventual separate commands are different stages.
